Charcot–Bouchard aneurysms are small microaneurysms that develop in the penetrating arteries, particularly in regions such as the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, and cerebellum. They are strongly associated with chronic hypertension and are a common cause of intracerebral haemorrhage, often resulting from the rupture of deep-seated arteries in the brain tissue.
The lenticulostriate branches (LSA) of the middle cerebral artery are commonly affected, leading to:

blocks.text: Berry aneurysms (Option A) are larger aneurysms located at the bifurcations of major cerebral arteries.

Rupture of these aneurysms can lead to subarachnoid haemorrhage, often associated with hypertension, causing bleeding between the arachnoid and pia mater. This condition typically presents as an extremely severe headache, often described as the worst headache of one's life.

**Mycotic aneurysm (Option B):** is caused by infection, often associated with endocarditis or other systemic infections, leading to weakened vessel walls and aneurysm formation. It presents with fever, localised pain, inflammation, and headaches.
**Rupture arteriovenous malformation (Option C):** may cause intracerebral hemorrhage but is less strongly associated with chronic hypertension and typically affects younger individuals.

Course of the spinal accessory nerve
Origin and Ascent within the Spinal Cord
Arises from motor neurons in the lateral aspect of the ventral horn of the cervical spinal cord (C1/2 to C5/6).
Rootlets combine to form the spinal accessory nerve trunk, ascend within the vertebral canal and enter the skull through the foramen magnum
Intracranial Course

Inside the skull, the nerve turns upward and moves laterally toward the jugular foramen. Travels through the jugular foramen in the same dural sheath as the vagus nerve, separated by a fold of arachnoid mater.
Extracranial Course and Branching
Exits the jugular foramen.

blocks.text: The inferior sagittal sinus is found between two meningeal layers in the free edge of the falx cerebri and not between the meningeal and endosteal layer of the dura.
Dural venous sinuses
Large, blood-filled spaces located within the dura mater of the cranial cavity & drain venous blood from the brain and the skull.
Formation
**Separation of Dura Layers:** They arise from the separation of the two layers of the dura mater—endosteal and meningeal layers.

**Reduplication of Meningeal Layer:** Some sinuses are formed by a duplication of the meningeal layer. Dural folds are formed by the folding of the meningeal layer and project into the cranial cavity.
Falx Cerebri
Extends vertically between the two cerebral hemispheres & contains the superior and inferior sagittal sinuses.
Tentorium Cerebelli
A horizontal fold that separates the cerebellum from the occipital lobes of the cerebrum. It contains the transverse sinuses along its margins.
Falx Cerebelli
Lies between the two cerebellar hemispheres & contains Occipital sinus.

The Inferior sagittal sinus and the Straight sinus are not located between the meningeal and endosteal layers of the dura mater. The inferior sagittal sinus is found in the free edge of the falx cerebri & straight sinus is located at the junction of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli.

The cavernous sinus contains the oculomotor nerve, trochlear nerve, ophthalmic nerve, maxillary nerve, and abducens nerve. The mandibular nerve does not pass through the cavernous sinus; it exits the skull via the foramen ovale.
**Cavernous Sinus:** Large venous space located on either side of the Sphenoid body & Sella turcica. Interior of the sinus is divided into smaller compartments (caverns) by trabeculae.
The floor is formed by the endosteal layer of the dura mater & lateral wall, roof, and medial wall are formed by the meningeal layer.

blocks.text: The superior sagittal sinus is an unpaired sinus located along the midline of the brain while others are paired sinuses, which exist in two symmetrical halves.
**Dural Venous Sinuses:** These are channels that drain blood from the brain and are located between the layers of the dura mater. They can be classified as 7 Paired & 7 Unpaired.
**Unpaired Sinuses:** Unpaired Sinuses

items.text: **Superior Sagittal Sinus:** Located along the midline, running from the front of the skull to the back. It collects blood from the brain's superficial structures.
**Inferior Sagittal Sinus:** Runs parallel to the superior sagittal sinus but is smaller and located lower. It drains blood from the deep structures of the brain.
**Straight Sinus:** Formed by the junction of the inferior sagittal sinus and the great cerebral vein. It drains into the confluence of sinuses.
**Occipital Sinus:** Located in the posterior cranial fossa, it drains the posterior part of the brain.
**Anterior Intercavernous Sinus:** Connects the two cavernous sinuses at the front, allowing for communication between them.
**Posterior Intercavernous Sinus:** Connects the cavernous sinuses at the back, also facilitating inter-sinus communication.
**Basilar Venous Plexus:** Drains blood from the brainstem and parts of the cerebellum.

blocks.text: **Paired Sinuses:** Paired Sinuses

items.text: **Transverse Sinus:** Located on either side of the brain, they drain blood from the superior sagittal sinus to the sigmoid sinuses.
**Sigmoid Sinus:** Continuations of the transverse sinuses, curve down to drain into the internal jugular veins.
**Superior Petrosal Sinus:** Located above the petrous part of the temporal bone, they drain blood from the cavernous sinus to the transverse sinuses.
**Inferior Petrosal Sinus:** Located near the base of the skull, they drain blood from the cavernous sinus directly into the internal jugular vein.
**Sphenoparietal Sinus:** Found along the lateral aspect of the sphenoid bone.
**Cavernous Sinus:** Paired structures located on either side of the sella turcica & contain cranial nerves and the internal carotid artery.
**Petrosquamous Sinus:** Lies in petrosquamous suture if present & drains into the transverse sinus.

blocks.text: The scenario with the given image findings indicates a Vein of Galen malformation, which involves the abnormal dilation of the vein formed by the union of the internal cerebral veins. In malformations, abnormal connections and dilations can occur, leading to significant clinical symptoms and complications such as hydrocephalus, developmental delays, seizures, congestive heart failure, headaches, neurological deficits.
**Great Cerebral Vein (Vein of Galen):** Single vessel Formed by union of thalamostriate, choroidal and septal vein, located beneath and posterior to the splenium of the corpus callosum.
Shortly after its formation, it receives blood from the two basal veins. Finally, it joins the inferior sagittal sinus to create the straight sinus.
**Tributaries of the Great Cerebral Vein:**

items.text: Internal cerebral veins
Basal veins
Veins from the colliculi (tectum of the midbrain)
Veins draining the cerebellum and adjacent regions of the occipital lobes of the cerebrum.

Nucleus Ambiguus Location and Function
The nucleus ambiguus is a motor nucleus.
It provides fibres to cranial nerves IX (Glossopharyngeal), X (Vagus), and the cranial root of XI (Accessory) nerve. (Option A, B, and C ruled out)

items.text: **Cranial Part:** Supplies muscles of the palate, pharynx, and larynx via cranial nerves IX, X, and XI.
